reference.source: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Painful audible or palpable snapping or grating (crepitus) of the scapula on the chest wall during shoulder movement
Arises at the scapulothoracic articulation, with scapulothoracic bursitis and/or bony or soft-tissue abnormalities at the medial and superomedial scapula
Often related to overuse in overhead and throwing activities and to scapular dyskinesis and posture
Causes include inflamed scapulothoracic bursae, muscle atrophy or fibrosis, and bony lesions such as osteochondroma or a prominent superomedial angle
Examination looks for crepitus, tenderness, scapular winging and dyskinesis
Imaging (radiographs, CT for bony lesions, MRI or ultrasound for soft tissue and bursae) is used when a structural cause is suspected

Most cases respond to conservative management with postural and scapular stabilisation rehabilitation, load modification and sometimes bursal injection; surgery is reserved for structural lesions or refractory bursitis
reference.pathophysiology: The scapula glides over the posterior chest wall at the scapulothoracic articulation, cushioned by bursae. Snapping scapula syndrome arises when this smooth gliding is disturbed, whether by inflamed or fibrotic scapulothoracic bursae, by altered muscle bulk or scarring, or by bony incongruity such as an osteochondroma, a prominent superomedial angle or a malunited rib or scapular fracture. Repetitive overhead loading, scapular dyskinesis and poor posture contribute. The result is symptomatic crepitus and pain as the scapula tracks over the chest wall.
additionalDifferentials: Osteochondroma or other bony lesion of the scapula or ribs
Long thoracic or spinal accessory nerve palsy causing scapular winging
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs including tangential scapular views
CT to define bony lesions such as an osteochondroma or a prominent angle
MRI or ultrasound to assess the bursae and soft tissues
Clinical assessment of scapular motion, winging and dyskinesis
Diagnostic bursal injection where scapulothoracic bursitis is suspected
redFlags: Fixed scapular winging suggesting a nerve palsy (long thoracic or spinal accessory)
A firm mass or rapidly growing lesion suggesting tumour
Night pain or systemic features suggesting neoplasm or infection
reference.prognosis: The majority improve with scapular rehabilitation and load management; outcomes are good after excision when a discrete bony lesion is the cause.
pitfalls: Attributing symptomatic crepitus to a benign cause without excluding an osteochondroma or other bony lesion
Missing a nerve palsy as a cause of associated winging
Neglecting scapular dyskinesis and posture in rehabilitation
Rushing to surgery before a trial of conservative care in non-structural cases
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: First-line scapular rehabilitation addressing scapular dyskinesis, posture and periscapular muscle strengthening, with load management.
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and corticosteroid injection into a symptomatic scapulothoracic bursa.
Scapulothoracic bursectomy for bursitis refractory to conservative care.
Excision of a discrete bony lesion such as an osteochondroma or a prominent superomedial angle, which gives good results.
Activity modification to reduce repetitive overhead and throwing loads.
Refer to sports medicine or shoulder surgery for persistent symptoms or a structural cause.
